# Write a finished Mo program

This page is the procedure for a finished Mo program. Correct Mo is Language Reference v0.1. `mo guide --reference` prints that reference. Section 13.4 says this guide covers how to work with the `mo` command, a small complete program with its tests, and when a task is done.

## Know this build

The language headings below use the present tense of the reference.

This build runs `mo check`, `mo run`, `mo test`, `mo format`, `mo fix`, `mo guide`, `mo emit`, `mo serve`, `mo fetch`, `mo push`, `mo review`, `mo replay`, `mo query`, `mo history` and `mo intent`. The program below checks with no errors, runs, and passes its examples and its test.

`mo fix FILE` makes each edit that `mo check` shows as an error's only fix, checks again, and prints the errors that are left, as `mo check` does. It rewrites only the files it is given.

`mo emit FILE -o OUT` checks the program as `mo check` does, then writes its bytecode to `OUT`. `-o` is required, and `OUT` is never a source file of the program. A module with neither `main` nor a service is E0079, as for `mo run`, and a file that cannot be written is E1404. This build has no command that runs a bytecode file; run the source with `mo run`.

This build checks, formats, fixes and serves `service ... end` blocks (reference 11.5). `mo test` never reads a service's token, and starts a service on its own only in the service's recovery check, below. Tests and examples can explicitly start one with `Simulation.start(Module, at)`, send registered tools with `Simulation.send(handle, Module.tool, args...)`, advance its fake clock, and crash/restart through the real log and snapshot path backed by an in-memory store. `send` returns the complete declared handler result inside another `Result`; an application `Error` is still inside `Ok`. Helpers may receive the handle. A promise whose inputs include a `Simulation` is E1400; promises over a service's sequences of steps are deferred. `mo run` on a service entry module still refuses with E1408, "mo run does not start services yet". Importing a service module does not start it.

`mo test` runs one recovery check for each service in the program, named after its module, such as `Counter.service.recovery` (reference 12.5). Its author writes nothing for it. It calls tools with generated arguments, advances the fake clock, crashes and restarts the service on an in-memory store, and checks that each restart recovers the state the service held before its crash. `--list` prints it after its module's other checks, and `--only` and `--in` select it. A service's own promises (reference 12.2) are checked on the same sequences. Each is named after its position, such as `Counter.service.promise.1`, listed just before the recovery check, and judged after every step it covers, restarts included. A failing promise prints its shrunk sequence with `broke` on the step that made it false, the states around that step and the condition that was false. Every service check runs its whole plan of 200 sequences, which `--calls` caps; `--seconds` does not apply. A promise body that runs past `MO_LIMIT_SERVICE_WORK` stops with that bug. For `counter.mo` under Run a service, `mo test counter.mo` prints `passed Counter.service.recovery  counter.mo:3:1`, then `1 passed, 0 failed, 0 stopped`. A failing check prints the numbered steps of a shrunk sequence, with literal arguments and each step's outcome, then the state before the crash and the state recovery produced. When the start value stops, the check stops with that bug.

`mo check --emit=bytecode FILE` prints the program's bytecode as indexed text, with a `services` section holding one descriptor for each module that declares a service, including imported modules. It works on a module without `main`. `mo emit FILE -o OUT` writes the same descriptors and accepts a service without `main`. Neither command evaluates a service's start value or reads its token, and `mo run` still does not start a service (E1408). `mo check --emit=core FILE` shows the start value and timer intervals as ordinary functions but no service registration, so Core output alone cannot reconstruct a service.

A service tool that returns exactly `State` or `Result(State, E)` gets E0101, "a service tool returns only its state". Only `(State, Reply)` and `Result((State, Reply), E)` save new state. `Option(State)`, `List(State)` and records containing state remain read-only replies. A `Result(State, E)` tool receives no fixes. For a bare `State` result, choose between returning `(state, Unit)` to save new state and returning the state inside a record as read-only data. `mo fix` applies neither alternative. The suggested adapters keep the tool's name and `##` comment, move the original function to a helper and rebind the module's references to that helper. Functions on the module's `expose` line receive no fixes because callers in other modules cannot be updated. Functions whose names end in `?` receive no fixes because a `?` name must still return `Bool`. A selected generic handler gets E0100, "a service handler is generic". State, handler inputs and handler results must contain neither capabilities nor function values; E0104 reports this restriction.

Service tool names cannot end in `?` (E0106). Tool arguments after State and Time, projected replies and application errors must have visible fields and cases, including nested types (E0105). Import a wire type with `(..)` to expose its representation. Private service state is not a wire type. E0101 takes precedence over these two checks.

`mo serve` connects a service to MCP clients over authenticated plain HTTP/1.1. HTTP policy, JSON-RPC validation and wire values run in embedded Mo; native code owns sockets, credentials and service dispatch. The transport's byte, node, work and memory ceilings are internal bounds, not language configuration. `mo run` still refuses a service entry module, and Simulation still provides no networking.

Authenticated MCP discovery lists author tools followed by `mo-overview`, `mo-state`, `mo-mailbox`, `mo-timers`, `mo-memory`, `mo-supervisor`, `mo-log`, `mo-export` and `mo-failures`, then the upgrade tools `mo-upgrade-open`, `mo-upgrade-page` and `mo-upgrade-commit`, which change the service and need a second credential, as Upgrade a running service says, the review tools `mo-intent-items`, `mo-intent-approve`, `mo-review-setting`, `mo-review-pending`, `mo-review-source` and `mo-review-answer`, which need a third, as Review intent says, and `mo-upgrade-status`, which needs the second. The same token grants access to private state. Only the nine operator views, `mo-intent-items`, `mo-review-pending`, `mo-review-source` and `mo-upgrade-status` are read-only; the three upgrade tools, `mo-intent-approve`, `mo-review-setting` and `mo-review-answer` carry `readOnlyHint: false`, and commit and `mo-review-answer` carry `destructiveHint: true`. These read-only operator views share the author-call rate limit and do not invoke handlers or enter the mailbox, recovery log or supervisor counts. `mo-state` accepts an optional `path` array of field names and indexes; bounded output marks truncation and `complete: false`, and a value too large to show becomes `{"truncated_bytes": N}` while the values after it still render. A list view that does not fit one reply reports `truncated`, the number of items left out, and `next`, the arguments for the following page: `mo-mailbox` and `mo-timers` take `offset`, `mo-supervisor` takes `after` and `before`, and `mo-log` takes `after`. Separate observations are not one atomic snapshot. `mo-log` retains committed message metadata only since the last snapshot; in-memory supervisor events disappear when the process exits. Live views need the endpoint URL and token, not shell access to the host. `mo-export` with `{"kind":"state"}` starts an immutable MOEX v1 state export; use the returned `next` arguments to read subsequent base64 pages. Each page identifies its export, durable recovery sequence and encoded-state sequence (which can differ after a snapshot failure). The final page releases the pin. A new export replaces the previous state export; 60 seconds without a page expires it. Refused generations never return another export’s bytes. Pins use native memory outside the handler heap. Fetch is available on the service host. `mo-failures` lists retained handler failures and current capture refusals; `after` selects the next record page. A handler failure reports `record: ID` or an explicit `record unavailable` reason before its reply. Application `Error` replies and admission refusals are excluded. Captures preserve pre-call state, arguments, arrival time, budgets, identity and bounded stack context; read-only failures never enter the recovery log. Retention keeps first/latest per kind, up to 64 records and 64 MiB of framed records. A repeating kind replaces its own latest record and never evicts another kind, so a repeat that does not fit is refused. A new kind evicts, as a whole, the kind whose latest record is oldest. Records survive snapshots. `mo-export` accepts `{"kind":"failure","failure":ID}` and has an independent failure pin. Run `mo fetch URL --export failure ID --out failure.moex --token-env NAME` for a verified private artifact. On the service host, `mo history`, `mo replay` and `mo query` read a stopped data folder or an artifact without starting the service, as Diagnose a failure offline says.

A few forms the reference requires are still unfinished. `mo check` reports E1103 for a form the checker has not implemented, with a headline that says so, such as "this constant's call dependencies are not implemented". It reports E1150 for a form it checks but cannot compile yet, such as a constant's function value that reads a later constant. The headline is "this constant's deferred function needs globals not yet initialized". E1103 and E1150 mean this toolchain has not implemented that form. `mo run` and `mo test` report the same code for the same form.

If the reference offers another way to write the same behaviour from forms that compile, use that instead. Keep the unfinished form only when the reference requires it and offers no other way to write the same behaviour.

Every `Int`, `Float` and `Bytes` function listed in reference section 14 compiles and runs, whether called with a dot, through its type's module, or as a function value. This includes checked, wrapping and saturating integer arithmetic, integer conversions, float rounding and classification, and UTF-8 decoding.

`Byte.to_int` and `List.sum` also compile and run through dot calls, module calls and function values. `sum` supports `Int`, `BigInt`, `Decimal` and `Float`, adds from the left, and returns the type's zero for an empty list. Integer and decimal overflow stop the program, as with `+`.

Every `BigInt` function in reference section 14 compiles and runs, including `abs`, `min`, `max`, `pow`, `floor_div`, `floor_mod` and `to_int`. `Random.int` and the fake constructor `Random.seeded` also compile, including as function values.

`T.to_text(x)` and `T.compare(a, b)` work as well as `x.to_text` and `a.compare(b)` for every type with `Text` or `Order`, written through the type (`Text.compare`, `Option.to_text`), a type parameter, or the module that declares the type (`Shapes.to_text`), and `T.to_text` and `T.compare` are function values. A case without fields can be the receiver directly, as in `Less.compare(Greater)` or `Folder.to_text`. `Ordering`, `Entry`, and `Map` support `to_text` and interpolation. Maps print entries in insertion order, with text and character keys and values quoted and escaped.

`Env.get` runs on real or fake capabilities. Tests, examples and promises can construct a fake with `Env.of`.

`mo test` exits 1 with E1400 when it cannot build the inputs of a selected promise, such as one whose function takes a function. The headline is "this build cannot generate inputs for this promise". Keep the promise. Run the other examples, promises and tests by name with `--only`, as `--list` prints them.

For a false promise, `mo test` shrinks hidden inputs by deleting builder calls and simplifying their arguments, never by editing hidden fields. Same-call companions stay whole. Builder and structural shrinking share 200 additional subject trials and the original deadline; the result is not guaranteed minimal. Each generated tuple can record at most 4096 builder recipes, including recipes made during unsuccessful starts. If recording runs out, generation continues unchanged. A passing tuple still passes; a failing tuple keeps its original counterexample and reports E1404 with the headline "promise shrinking is limited because builder recording is incomplete".

For a promise on a generic function, `mo test` generates and shrinks inputs for every concrete instantiation already in the program, including anchors and program uses. It keeps complete type-argument lists, without cross-products or default types. `--list` and `--only` use the source promise's name. Each concrete instance has a separate result and counts separately in the totals. Its text result names the instance, and its JSON result adds an `instance` field with the concrete name and types. An unsupported instance refuses the selected set before initialization or tests run.

`mo test --list --json` gives each promise, service promise and example row a `digest`: a SHA-256 of its own text and of every declaration it reads, so it changes only when what judges the code changes. `mo test FILE --strength DIR` measures how many wrong versions the intent kills. It runs the program's own checks first, then each `.mo` file in `DIR`, which replaces named declarations of one module, against the same checks on the same fixed plan, and prints one `strength` record. Its rate counts the versions a promise or an example kills; a version that only a test or a recovery check kills is `killed_by_test`, counted in `killed_any` but not in the rate. A wrong version that stops is kept out of the rate, and so is one that does not check or changes a digest, unless a `counted` file in `DIR` lists it: a listed one stays in the rate as not killed. A plan cut short by `--seconds` exits 1 with E1432, "the plan did not finish".

`mo test FILE --gates` also tries mutants of the program. A mutant is one small change to the code of a function in `FILE` or in a program module it imports: a comparison moved to its boundary or negated, `and` swapped with `or`, a `not` removed, `+` swapped with `-` or `*` with `/`, a Bool flipped, or an Int raised by one. The checks run first, with no clock. If one fails, it is reported as without `--gates` and no mutant is tried. Next, each function on the `expose` line of those modules, other than `main`, needs a promise or an example of its own, each overload on its own, and each service tool needs a service promise `on` it or a promise or an example of its own; a step promise does not count. Each one without is an error, E1440, "an exposed function states no intent" or "a service tool states no intent", and no mutant is tried. Then each mutant runs against the checks that ran its function, cheapest first, and is killed when one of them no longer passes or the program no longer starts. Each mutant that survives is an error, E1439, "a mutant survived: no check noticed this change", which names the function, the line and the change, and says when no check runs that function at all. A mutant that does not check is dropped. Before the totals line, a `gates:` line counts the mutants tried, those killed by each kind of check and at start, those that survived and those dropped. With `--only`, `--in`, `--calls`, `--seconds` or a `--max` limit, the checks run as without `--gates`, no mutant is tried, and the line says `gates: did not run`. With `--json`, each mutant tried or dropped is also a `mutant` record giving its function, place, kind and change, its `outcome` (`killed`, `survived` or `dropped`), the kind of check that killed it as `by` and that check's full name as `check`. `mo test FILE --gates --list` runs nothing: after the checks' names it prints each mutant as `mutant FILE:LINE:COLUMN NAME: CHANGE` and each function of those modules as `function NAME: N mutants`, as `mutant` and `function` records with `--json`. `--gates` takes no `--bundle` or `--strength`.

`mo test FILE --against OLD` is a shorter gated run against the previous version, where `OLD` is that version's copy of `FILE` (for a library module, its folder is the library). Both versions must check; the checks of both run first. Only the mutants of functions whose code changed, that are new, or that a changed check ran are tried. A check changed when it is gone, renamed, has other text, reads a test-only helper that changed, or no longer runs the function. Every other function is carried over, and a line before the counts says `gates: not the full run: N functions carried over untried from previous version DIGEST`, the SHA-256 of the source bundle `mo push` would send. Before it, the change summary lists `change: no longer true: NAME`, `change: newly true: NAME`, `change: about something new: NAME` and `change: could not be compared: NAME: REASON`, then one `changes against previous version DIGEST:` line with the counts, including the checks that pass on both. A check in one version only is put into the other program and run there. The summary never changes the exit status: read "no longer true" and "could not be compared" yourself. With `--json` each entry is a `change` record, the counts a `changes` record, and the totals say `"gates":"ran shorter"` with `carried` and `previous`. An `OLD` that does not check is an error naming its first diagnostic. `--against` takes no selector, `--calls`, `--seconds`, `--max` limit, `--list`, `--bundle` or `--strength`.

`mo intent FILE` lists the program's intent without its code: each promise and service promise with its sentence, conditions and anchors, each function's example rows as a table, and each item's digest and the declarations it reads. `mo intent FILE --against OLD` shows how the intent changed since the program `OLD`: items edited, with both texts, removed, added and moved to another function, and for an edited or moved item each declaration it reads that changed, before and after. Unchanged items are only counted. A read of one overload of a function is named with `@` and the type it is called on, as in `Main.score@Point`. With `--json` each item or change is one record, followed by an `intent` record with the counts; its `items` counts the program `FILE`.

The `lib/` folder holds library modules written in Mo, and every `mo` command loads them with your program. `mo check lib/list.mo` and `mo test lib/list.mo` check and test one of them on its own. `lib/list.mo` has `List`'s `map`, `filter`, `filter_map`, `flat_map`, `reduce`, `find`, `any?`, `all?`, `count`, `sort_by`, `sort_by_desc`, `sort`, `min`, `max` and `group_by`, `lib/map.mo` has `Map.update`, `lib/option.mo` has `Option.or_fail` and `Option.map`, `lib/result.mo` has `Result.map` and `Result.map_error`, `lib/file-error.mo` has `FileError.to_text`, `lib/json.mo` is the `Json` module (`use Json`, then `Json.parse`, `to_text` and `pretty`), and `lib/files.mo` and `lib/read-files.mo` have `walk` for `Files` and `ReadFiles`. `lib/text.mo` has no functions, only tests of `Text`'s operations, written from reference section 14 and run by `mo test lib/text.mo`. `lib/set.mo` likewise tests `Set`'s operations, `List.to_set` and Set text forms with `mo test lib/set.mo`. `lib/unicode16.mo` is the `Unicode16` module. After `use Unicode16`, its built-in `graphemes`, `display_width`, `normalize_nfc`, `lowercase` and `uppercase` operations follow Unicode 16.0. `mo test lib/unicode16.mo` tests them. `lib/time.mo` has no functions, only tests of `Time`'s, `Duration`'s and `Clock.fixed`'s operations, run by `mo test lib/time.mo`. The rest of section 14 is still built in. Section 10.5 names what is always in scope.

After `use Unicode16`, `Unicode16.letter?(c: Char) : Bool` tests Unicode 16.0 General_Category L (`Lu`, `Ll`, `Lt`, `Lm`, `Lo`), and `Unicode16.digit?(c: Char) : Bool` tests `Nd` (decimal digits). Neither includes `Nl`, `No` or marks, normalizes, or uses locale tailoring. For example, `text.chars.filter(fn(c) Unicode16.letter?(c) or Unicode16.digit?(c) end)` keeps letters and decimal digits.

After `use Json` (or `use Shop.Account`), a bare `Json` (or `Account`) in a type is the module's own type of that name, as reference 10.3 says: write `fn f(value: Json)`. `Json.Json` means the same type.

## Write this program

Use this shape.

```mo
## Greets the name given on the command line, or the world.
module Greet

fn greeting(name: Option(Text)) : Text
  examples
    greeting(Some("Ada")) == "Hello, Ada!"
    greeting(None) == "Hello, world!"
  end

  "Hello, #{name or "world"}!"
end

fn main(args: Args, console: Console)
  console.print(greeting(args.list.first))
end

test "only the first argument is used"
  console = Console.fake()
  main(Args.of(["Ada", "Grace"]), console)
  assert console.printed == ["Hello, Ada!"]
end
```

The `##` comment documents the module, and the module line names `Greet`. Sections 1 and 2.2.

`greeting` types its parameter and its result. Inside a body, types are inferred from all their uses in it. The body's value is the value of its last line. Section 5.1.

`name` is an `Option`. `Some` and `None` are its cases, and `name or "world"` gives the value inside `Some`, or `"world"` for `None`. Sections 3 and 8.1.

`"Hello, #{name or "world"}!"` inserts the text form of that value. Section 3.4.

`main` lists the capabilities the program needs, here `Args` and `Console`. Sections 11.1 and 11.2.

`examples` sits at the top of the body, then a blank line, then the code. Sections 12 and 12.1.

The `test` uses `Console.fake()`, `Args.of`, and `console.printed`. Sections 12.3 and 12.4.

`args.list.first` calls `first` with no other arguments. This file has no `promise`. Sections 5.4 and 12.2.

## Follow these rules

Write these forms. The section number states the rule.

- Where another language writes `items[i]` or `map[key]`, write `items.get(i)` or `map.get(key)`. `get` returns an `Option`. Sections 3.7 and 3.8.
- Bind a name once with `name = value`. A name is visible from its binding to the end of its block. To assign it again, declare `var name = value` where it is first bound, even when the assignment is inside a loop or a branch. Sections 6.1 and 6.2.
- Join texts by inserting them into one text, as in `"#{name}: #{score}"`. `+` adds numbers and does not join texts. Section 3.4.
- A list's length is `list.size`. A text's is `text.char_count` or `text.byte_count`. There is no `len` or `length`. Sections 3.4 and 14.
- Add an element with `items = items.append(x)`, and declare `var items` when you assign that name again. Sections 3.7 and 6.2.
- Mo has no exceptions, and there is no "unwrap". Return `Error(...)`, pass it on with `try`, and handle it with `case`. Where a failure truly cannot happen, write `stop` and the reason. Sections 8.2, 8.3, and 8.4.
- Cover every possible value in a `case`. On a choice, a whole arm cannot be `_` or a name, so list the cases. Inside a pattern, `_` or a name may stand for anything. Section 7.2.
- Pass a capability in only as a parameter. Make a fake only in tests, examples, and promises. Sections 11 and 12.4.
- Declare a `struct` or an `enum`. Records have no methods. Put functions in that module. Sections 4 and 5.4.
- To state that a function holds for every input, write a `promise` with a sentence, a body, an `allows` line, and a `forbids` line. Section 12.2.
- When another module needs a name, list it with `expose` and bring the module in with `use`. Section 10.

The program `Shout` in section 1 has no `examples` and no `promise`.

Pass function arguments by position. Only records and cases are built with named fields. Section 5.2.

- Section 3 is values and types, including the sample's text and lists. Mo never converts between types silently.
- Section 4 is a `struct` or an `enum`.
- Section 5 is recursion, generic functions, and functions as values. There are no default or optional parameters.
- Section 6 is a name bound once, and `var` for a later assignment.

164	## Run a service
165	
166	`mo serve FILE --port N --data DIR [--allow-host NAME]` runs the service that the module in `FILE` declares. Check three things first:
167	
168	- `FILE` has a `service` block. Without one, `mo serve` refuses with E1409, "this module has no service to start". An imported service does not count.
169	- `DIR` exists. `mo serve` never creates it, so a mistyped path cannot start an empty service. Saved state goes in `DIR/service.sqlite`. `service.sqlite` is readable only by its owner. Only one `mo serve` can use a `DIR` at a time.

172	`--port` takes 0 to 65535. Port 0 picks a free port. `mo serve` listens on 127.0.0.1 only. 223	`mo serve` writes one line to standard error for each failure, restart and stop, in exactly these formats:
224	
225	```text
226	mo serve: failure: NAME: REASON
227	mo serve: restart: N of M: REASON
228	mo serve: stop: REASON
229	```

231	`NAME` is the tool or timer that failed, as the source writes it, such as `halt` or `tick`. A bad interval names its timer. A saved message that replay runs and rejects, because its handler failed or its result failed the checksum, names its tool or timer. A record refused before it runs, because it is malformed, out of sequence or from a different program, is `service`. `NAME` is the word `service` when no tool or timer is responsible, as when the state's initial value fails, or the store or saved data fails at startup. `mo check` refuses `service` as a tool or timer name, so the word never means a real handler. `NAME` never holds a colon, and `REASON` is always one line. A store that will not open is E1409 with no `failure` line. A store another process holds, such as a second `mo serve` or a reader of `DIR`, is not E1409: `mo serve` waits up to 10 seconds for it, then prints one `mo serve: could not open saved state at` line and exits 75. `N` is this restart's place among the restarts of the last ten minutes, and `M` is the limit of 3, so `3 of 3` is followed by the stop line. A store failure while the service runs is a `stop` line with no `failure` line. A failure that is a bug adds the report `mo run` would print after its line, except during replay. The report's values can quote these words, so anchor a search as `^mo serve: failure:`. Read journald with `journalctl -o cat`, so each line keeps its start. The lines have no timestamps. These line shapes are stable, and changing one is a breaking change. The words of `REASON` are not stable, so branch on the line's kind, on `NAME` and on the exit status. The token never appears in output, logs or errors.

233	`mo serve` exits with one of these statuses:
234	
235	- 0: SIGTERM or SIGINT stopped it. It closes its port, so a new connection is refused, and finishes the open ones first, which their deadlines bound to about 25 seconds.
236	- 1: the program has errors, or it could not start (E1409).
237	- 2: a mistake in the command.
238	- 69: supervision (D308) stopped the service. Five failures within a minute restart it, and three restarts within ten minutes stop it. It stays down until a person starts it, as Recover from a stop says.
239	- 70: it died any other way, such as a failed save, a listener failure or a bug in a module constant. Starting it again is safe.
240	- 75: another process held the store for the whole wait. Nothing was changed, and starting it again is safe, so a service manager should retry it.

242	`DIR` records the canonical source bundle, its digest, and the build and state identities alongside the saved state. The first `mo serve FILE --data DIR --port N` records the program atomically with its initial snapshot. Thereafter `mo serve --data DIR --port N` compiles the recorded program and starts it. Supplying `FILE` requires the same source digest; any source-byte change, including comments, needs an explicit upgrade. Moving the same files does not change their source identity. A new executable build must verify every replayed state checksum before recording its build identity, even if the service image key is unchanged. The previous program identity is retained so failures captured under either build remain attributable. A recorded program that no longer compiles is refused; keep the recording executable for recovery.

244	A legacy folder with no recorded program can be adopted when its compiled image matches. For a different image, `--adopt` explicitly permits verified replay. An empty tail verifies zero messages and provides no evidence about changed handler behavior. Adoption is not a substitute for migrating an incompatible state schema.

246	## Recover from a stop
247	
248	After status 69, read the `mo serve: failure:` lines and their reports to find the handler that failed. Stop callers that repeatedly send the failing message before restarting.
249	
250	- Restart the recorded program with `mo serve --data DIR --port N`.
251	- Check a candidate with `mo check NEW --upgrade-from OLD [--migrate Module.function] [--json]`. `OLD` can be a standalone source file or a stopped service data folder. Use the folder after a prior migration so the check can read its recorded source and validated generated declarations. The check does not write to the folder. Exit 0 means the source and migration signature checks passed; it does not mean a migration ran over the folder's state.
252	- With the service stopped, run `mo serve NEW --data DIR --port N --upgrade [--migrate Module.function] [--review ID]`. Matching saved schemas need no migration. A changed schema needs a pure, non-generic function taking exactly one old state and returning exactly the new service state. Import generated old declarations from `UpgradeOld`; they come from the recorded program, never a candidate disk module. Changed access clauses are refused.
253	
254	The checked restart runs the same checks as a push, refusing a failure with E1433 and an unfinished plan with E1432. The review setting then decides as it does for a push: when it would hold the upgrade, the restart prints the intent difference and the review id and refuses with E1435 unless `--review ID` names that id. Every refusal leaves the old program active. The checked restart replays the old state, runs the migration within restart budgets, validates the result and records the new program and snapshot in one activation transaction. A refused migration leaves the old program and state authoritative. After a successful activation, folder-only startup runs the new program without rerunning the migration. Generated old declarations needed to compile it are retained with the program separately from its source identity, including across later tool-only upgrades. Use it for a migration the live budget refuses.
255	
256	Source-only `mo check` and `mo test` do not automatically load a recorded program's generated `UpgradeOld` declarations. Use a data-folder base for upgrade checks. `mo replay --failure ID --data DIR` without `FILE` replays a failure under the program the folder retained for it, chosen by image key, build and schema, with its generated declarations. When retained programs with different sources match, it refuses with E1431; give `FILE` then.

258	## Upgrade a running service
259	
260	Start the service with a second and a third credential: `mo serve --data DIR --port N --upgrade-token-env NAME --approval-token-env NAME`. Each value must be at least 16 bytes, and the service token and the two credentials must all differ, or the service does not start (E1434); `--upgrade-token-env` without `--approval-token-env` is refused the same way. Without `--upgrade-token-env` every upgrade tool call is refused with E1414. The service token alone never authorizes an upgrade, and neither credential appears in output, events or the data folder.
261	
262	On the service host, or through a loopback tunnel to it, run `mo push NEW --url http://127.0.0.1:N/mcp --base DIGEST --token-env NAME --upgrade-token-env NAME [--migrate Module.function] [--json]`. The URL must be plain HTTP to a loopback address; any other URL is refused before either credential is read. `DIGEST` is the source digest of the active program: `mo check NEW --upgrade-from OLD --json` prints it as `base_source`, and a push naming the wrong base is refused with E1416 naming the active digest. The push uploads the source bundle, which the service compiles in a child process while it keeps serving. Two more child processes then list its intent items and run every promise, service promise, example and test in the modules the bundle carries under a fixed plan: 200 inputs per function promise and 1,000 sequences per service, with no clock cutting any check short: only the whole run's limits, 120 seconds of CPU and 180 seconds in all, stop it. A failure is refused with E1433, naming the failing item, and a plan that does not finish with E1432. The review setting then decides, as Review intent says: under `everything` every push is held, and under `intent` a push is held unless it keeps every approved item, still calls the function each one is about from a tool, a timer or the state initializer, and names no migration. A held push exits 3 and prints `held` and its review id, and the old program keeps serving. Otherwise the service checks the candidate against the running program as the checked restart does, migrates the current state under the live budget (1,048,576 work units, 32 MiB), and activates it between two messages in one transaction. Queued calls continue under the new program in order; a queued call to a tool the candidate removed or retyped is answered with the runtime error `removed_by_upgrade` and has no effect; a queued tick of a removed timer is dropped. Timers keep their next due time by name. Exit 0 means the service runs the candidate; the report gives the activation `ordinal`. Pushing the active program again reports `already active` and changes nothing, so a push whose reply was lost is safe to repeat. Exit 1 means a refusal or client failure; exit 2 means invalid command usage, URL or base digest; exit 3 means the push is held for review. A refusal names its E14xx code and leaves the old program serving. After activation there is no rollback: a fault in the new program is fixed by another push or, with the service stopped, a checked restart.
263	
264	The three children run confined where the host can confine them: Linux with Landlock ABI 3 or later (kernel 6.2) and seccomp. Each child reads only the `mo` executable, `lib/`, the system libraries and its inputs, writes only its own folder, opens no socket and signals no other process. On a host that cannot confine, such as macOS, `mo serve` accepts no upgrade. Started with an upgrade or approval credential, it prints `mo serve: upgrades: refused, because this host cannot confine the compile children; --unconfined accepts upgrades unconfined` on standard error, and a push, or `mo serve NEW --upgrade` with changed source, is refused with E1438. Add `--unconfined` to accept upgrades there anyway. The start line is then `mo serve: upgrades: the compile children are not confined (--unconfined)`, a JSON report adds `"confined":false`, and a text report adds the line `the compile children were not confined (--unconfined)`. Where the host can confine, `--unconfined` changes nothing.
265	
266	Initialize returns an `MCP-Session-Id`. A client that sends it on `GET /mcp` with `Accept: text/event-stream` receives `notifications/tools/list_changed` after each activation; each session has one stream, and a new GET replaces it. Notifications are not a durable log: a reconnecting client calls `tools/list`. POST calls work with or without the session header.

268	If a checked restart is refused and the program cannot be repaired within those checks, use the fresh-folder fallback. Start the old program on the old `DIR`, read what you need through its tools, and stop it. Start the fixed program on a new, empty `DIR` and send that data to its tools. State that no tool returns stays behind, so keep the old source, executable and data folder.

270	## Review intent
271	
272	Robert approves a program's intent items one by one; an agent cannot. The approval credential is his, and a request that carries it together with the upgrade credential is refused, so holding the service token and the upgrade credential never approves anything. Run `mo review --url http://127.0.0.1:N/mcp --token-env NAME --approval-token-env NAME` with one of `--items`, which lists the active program's items with their digests, each marked approved or unapproved, `--base PROGRAM --approve DIGEST...`, which approves those items of the active program `PROGRAM`, or `--setting everything|intent`, which sets what a later upgrade will ask Robert to review. A wrong or missing approval credential is E1414, a `PROGRAM` that is not the active one or a digest it lacks is E1416, and a full review record is E1437. An activation keeps the approvals of the items it leaves unchanged and drops the rest, so an edited or removed item is unapproved until Robert approves its new content, and an added one starts unapproved. `mo history DIR` prints the setting, the approvals and every decision.
273	
274	A held upgrade waits for Robert. `mo-review-pending` shows its review id and its intent difference: each approved item it lacks, each approved item whose function no tool, timer or state initializer calls any more, marked `not reached`, beside the items it adds on the same owner. `mo review ... --yes ID` compiles and checks it again, activates it between two messages, approves the edited and added items it showed and drops the approval of each item it showed `not reached`; `--no ID` drops it and leaves the old program serving. `mo review ... --out DIR` prints the intent difference, writes the held source tree to `DIR/pending` and the active one to `DIR/active`, and prints `review ID` last; it offers no id when the held upgrade changes while it reads or the source does not hash to the digests the id binds. An ID that is not the held upgrade's is E1435, which names the current one, and nothing held is E1436. A later held push replaces the earlier one, and any activation, including a checked restart, or approval makes it stale, so its ID answers nothing; a setting change leaves it held, and a restart without `--upgrade` keeps it. `mo-upgrade-status`, under the service token and the upgrade credential, shows the held upgrade's id and state and the latest decisions, without source.

276	## Work on a service behind the door
277	
278	A service behind the door runs on its own host, and you reach it only through its endpoint, over a tunnel that reaches its port and nothing else. You have no shell on the host and no access to its data folder. Through the tunnel you can call its tools and operator views, push with `mo push`, read the door's state with `mo-upgrade-status`, fetch an export with `mo fetch`, and replay or query a fetched export with the same `mo` build and the deployed source. `mo history`, replay and query on the data folder, the journal's failure reports, and anything after the service stops need the host, so they need Robert, and so do a restart on a new program and a start in a fresh data folder. When the service stops, tell Robert; you cannot restart it. Never ask for the approval credential or keep it in your shell or client configuration.
279	
280	The lock does not protect against a shell on the service's host or write access to its data folder, which carry approval authority as well as upgrade authority. Nor does it protect against a memory-safety defect in the compiler or the VM that pushed source can reach, a change to a library module or the toolchain that changes what an approved item means while its digest stays the same, or a defect outside the generated sequences the door checks on every push. Tests are not approved intent.

385	| `CHECK` | What differs | What to do |
386	| --- | --- | --- |
387	| `format` | The artifact or record cannot be read, is not a regular file, or its state does not belong to its message | Fetch the artifact again, or copy the stopped folder again |
388	| `kind` | A state export given with `--failure`, or a failure without it | Fetch the other kind, or add or drop `--failure ID` |
